title: Docs that start from the job
metaTitle: Docs that open on the job to do
excerpt: Open documentation on the task someone is trying to finish. Reference material belongs after a path that works, not as a sidebar of every noun.
alt: A white geometric building with a glass wing and a cantilevered upper volume, a structure with a clear entrance for an article about docs that start from the job.
caption: A building you can enter without a map of every room. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How should a documentation site be organized?
faqs.answer: Lead with the jobs people come to finish, each as a short path with a result. Put reference, such as every field and every error code, behind that path or in a separate section labeled as reference. A sidebar that lists every noun in the product makes the reader build the path themselves.

faqs.question: What belongs on the first docs page?
faqs.answer: The first page should name who the docs are for and offer the three or four jobs they most often have. A long welcome essay and a diagram of the whole system delay the task. Link the changelog and the status page from here, and keep them from replacing the task pages.

faqs.question: When should you add search?
faqs.answer: Add search when the set is too long to scan, and show the heading that matched, not only the page title. Until then, clear job titles are the finding tool. A search box on five pages is a decoration. A search box on a warehouse of nouns is an apology for the structure.

markdown:
Documentation information architecture should open on the job a person is trying to finish. The path that works comes first. A dictionary of every object in the product comes after, for the person who already knows which object they need.

A sidebar of every noun is a warehouse. Warehouses are useful to the people who stock them. They are a poor front door for someone with a task and a deadline.

## Start from the job, not the schema

List the jobs you actually hear. Invite a teammate. Export the Friday report. Connect the account that sends email. Recover when a payment fails. Those sentences are the table of contents. The database tables are not.

Each job page has a result in the first paragraph. "By the end of this page you will have sent a test invite." Then the steps, in order, with the words from the interface. Then the two failures people hit, and how to tell them apart. Reference links sit at the bottom, labeled, so a hurried reader can stop when the job is done.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a page has a primary purpose someone came for. A doc page's purpose is the job. A page that exists to define a noun, with no path through it, is a glossary entry. Glossaries are allowed. They should not be the navigation.

Write the title of the page as the job. "Invite a teammate" can be forwarded in a chat. "Team resource" cannot. [The same clarity WCAG asks of an interface](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/), that people can perceive structure and understand what to do, applies to the docs. Headings should be headings. Steps should be a list. A paragraph that hides step three in the middle of a story will be misread, and the misreading will become a support ticket.

## A path that works, then the reference

The path uses the real UI. Button names. The screen they are on. What they should see if it worked. If a step depends on a role, say the role in the step, not in a footnote three pages away. Screenshots help when the screen is crowded. Crop to the control. Replace them when the control moves, or delete them. A stale crop is worse than none, because it sends people to a button you renamed.

After the path, link the reference they might need next. The list of roles. The list of limits. The error codes for this job only, not every error the platform has ever emitted. A reader who wants the warehouse can have a reference section. They should have to choose it. They should not be dropped into it because the sidebar had nowhere else to put "Role."

Keep one example that runs through related jobs. The same workspace, the same two people, the same Friday report. Readers build a mental model from continuity. A docs site that invents a new fictional company on every page makes them relearn the cast instead of the task.

Code samples, if you have an API, follow the same order. The call that completes the job. Then the fields. Then the errors for that call. A reference generated from types is a fine appendix. It is a hostile homepage. Put a human path in front of it, even if the path is short.

## The sidebar is a map, not a dump

A useful sidebar answers "where do I go for this job." It can group jobs by the kind of person: an admin, a teammate, a developer. It should not list sixty pages at the same level. People do not choose well from sixty siblings. They choose from a handful, then go deeper.

Collapse reference under its own heading. Getting started, if you need it, should be one page that points at the first job, not a cluster of philosophy. Release notes can link to the changelog. Incidents belong on the status page. Mixing those three jobs into one tree teaches people that the docs are where you wander.

Name pages for the reader. Internal project names can stay in the repository. The visible title and the title in the navigation should match the heading on the page. A mismatch here is how people think the link is broken. It also confuses search, inside the site and outside it.

Review the tree with someone who did not write it. Give them a job and watch. If they open three wrong pages, the labels are wrong, even if the content of the right page is excellent. Fix the label before you add more pages. More pages make a bad map worse.

## Writing the page so it can be maintained

Give every page an owner and a "last reviewed" date you are willing to honor. Docs rot when the feature changes and the page does not. A date from two years ago, on a page that describes the current button, is an accident waiting for a suspicious reader. If you cannot review it, mark it, or remove it.

Write steps as steps. Short lines. One action each. The explanation of why can be a sentence under the step, not a preface that delays it. People in a hurry will skip the preface and then do the step wrong. People with time will still read a sentence under the action.

Say what you will not cover. "This page is for the admin invite. Members cannot send invites." That sentence prevents a whole class of confused tickets. It is also kinder than letting them finish the steps and fail at the end.

Link like a person who has used the product. "See invite roles" with the destination obvious. "Click here" is not a link name, and it fails the same understandability bar as an unlabeled button. The link text should say what they will get.

On a Hanabi build, docs that sit beside a product in Next.js and React should be editable by the people who ship the change. A markdown file in the repository, or a small CMS the team will actually open, beats a wiki nobody has the password for. The client portal can hold the decision. The public doc has to hold the path.

## The first page, and the pages you refuse

The docs homepage is a directory of jobs, plus one sentence on who it is for. Three to five jobs. A link to reference. A link to contact or to the community, if a human is part of the support plan. A search box only if the body is large enough that scanning will fail.

Refuse pages that exist because a stakeholder wanted a presence. A vision page. A glossary of marketing terms. A duplicate of the homepage hero. Each of those pushes a real job one row down. The reader came with a task. Honor that, and they will forgive a plain visual design.

Refuse orphan pages. If a page is not linked from a job or from the reference index, it is a trap for search and a burden to update. Either give it a parent or delete it. A search result that lands on an orphan feels like a different product.

Trade Moai and Leadly, as public interfaces, show how a screen can be organized around a scan. Docs deserve the same courtesy. One hierarchy. The next action visible. No pile of equal cards that all say "learn."

## When the docs and the product drift

Drift starts with a rename. The button changed on Tuesday. The doc still says the old verb. The user thinks they are in the wrong place. The fix is a habit: the change is not done until the path that mentions it is updated, or explicitly checked and left alone. Put that check on the release list next to the changelog entry.

Drift also starts with a second audience. Developers arrive, and someone adds a reference dump to the top of a user guide. Admins arrive, and the member path grows warnings that scare members. Split the audiences in the navigation when their jobs diverge. Do not blend the warnings into one page and hope the right person feels addressed.

If you cannot keep the docs current, shrink them. Five true paths beat thirty nostalgic ones. Say, on the homepage, that these are the supported tasks. A smaller true set is a position. A large stale set is a reputation.

Read a path yourself on a clean account every so often. Your own admin brain will skip steps your users cannot skip. The clean account is the editor. Time the path. If it takes you ten minutes and the page claims two, the page is advertising.

## The limit of a perfect tree

No structure removes the need for a human on the weird case. Docs should make the common jobs fast and the edge cases findable. They should also tell the person when to stop reading and ask. A contact path on a failed search, and on the bottom of a long reference page, is part of the architecture. A docs site that cannot admit confusion will be blamed for it anyway.

The sibling concern is what you publish when the product is down, which is not a doc and not a changelog. [Status pages and the trust around them](/blog/status-pages-and-the-trust-around-them) covers what to say while something is broken. Link that page from the docs, and do not make readers hunt the footer during an incident.

If you want the public site and the docs to share one structure a team will keep, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). Bring the current sidebar. The useful work is deciding which labels are jobs, and which are only nouns.
